notes.front: What is a sub-issue on GitHub?
notes.back: An issue added beneath another issue to break the work down, so you can browse the full hierarchy of work to be done.
notes.explanation: Issues already track work; sub-issues add a hierarchy to that work that you can browse from the top.
notes.example: Like a checklist inside an issue, but each item is an issue in its own right, sitting under the parent.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About issues”
notes.evidence: You can also break your work down further by adding sub-issues and easily browse the full hierarchy of work to be done.

notes.front: What is an issue dependency on GitHub?
notes.back: A blocking relationship between issues: it shows which issues are blocked by, or are blocking, other work.
notes.explanation: It records an order between pieces of work, not a parent and child, which is what sub-issues record.
notes.example: Like a sub-issue link, but saying “this cannot move until that is done” rather than “this is part of that”.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About issues”, “About issue dependencies”
notes.evidence: You can define blocking relationships between issues using issue dependencies. Issue dependencies let you identify issues that are blocked by, or blocking, other work.

notes.front: What is the Azure Boards and GitHub integration?
notes.back: A connection between GitHub repositories and an Azure Boards project, so GitHub code activity can be linked to work items.
notes.explanation: You can set it up from either side, and it works with GitHub.com and GitHub Enterprise Server repositories.
notes.example: Like linking a GitHub issue from a pull request, but the other end of the link is an Azure Boards work item.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is the Azure Boards-GitHub integration?”, “Integration between Azure Boards and GitHub” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Boards and Azure DevOps support integration with GitHub.com and GitHub Enterprise Server repositories. You can start from either Azure Boards or GitHub to integrate and connect to GitHub repositories to an Azure Boards project.

notes.front: What is the Azure Boards app for GitHub?
notes.back: The GitHub app recommended for connecting GitHub.com repositories to Azure Boards; it authenticates and operates as the app, not as a person.
notes.explanation: The documentation also credits it with a more streamlined configuration experience.
notes.example: Like a shared service account doing the linking, instead of one developer’s personal GitHub sign-in.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is the Azure Boards-GitHub integration?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you want to configure and manage your connections to GitHub.com, use the Azure Boards app for GitHub. The app provides a more streamlined configuration experience and has the advantage of authenticating and operating as the app rather than an individual.

notes.front: What is the `AB#` mention syntax?
notes.back: Writing `AB#` and a work item ID, such as `AB#125`, in GitHub text to link to that Azure Boards work item.
notes.explanation: You add it to a commit message, a pull request description or an issue description.
notes.example: Like typing `#12` to link GitHub issue 12, but `AB#12` points at Azure Boards work item 12.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Link GitHub commits, pull requests, branches, and issues to work items in Azure Boards”, “Use AB# to link from GitHub to Azure Boards work items” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use `AB#` mentions in GitHub text to link to Azure Boards work items. To create a link: 1. Add `AB#{ID}` to a commit message, pull request description, or issue description.

notes.front: What is the Development section of a work item?
notes.back: The part of the work item form that opens the branches, commits, pull requests and builds linked to it.
notes.explanation: For GitHub repositories it can also show Integrated in build links, once automatic linking is switched on in the `YAML` pipeline settings.
notes.example: Like the “linked issues” box on a GitHub pull request, but on the work item, listing code objects instead.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About end-to-end traceability”, “Deploy changes into production” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Development section: Open branches, commits, pull requests, or builds linked to the work item. For GitHub repositories, Integrated in build links are also shown in this section when you enable the automatic linking option in your YAML pipeline settings.
introduces: Development section of a work item
uses: Development section of a work item

notes.front: What are GitHub pull request insights on a work item?
notes.back: Extra status details shown beside a linked GitHub pull request in the work item’s Development section.
notes.explanation: They let you assess the pull request’s progress without opening it in GitHub.
notes.example: Like the checks summary on a GitHub pull request page, but seen from the Azure Boards work item.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Link GitHub commits, pull requests, branches, and issues to work items in Azure Boards”, “GitHub pull request insights” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Linked GitHub pull requests in the Development section show extra status details. You can assess progress without opening the pull request in GitHub.
introduces: GitHub pull request insights on a work item
uses: GitHub pull request insights on a work item
Development section of a work item

notes.front: What is end-to-end traceability in Azure DevOps?
notes.back: Linking the objects of the development process, from work items through code to builds and releases, so work can be followed throughout.
notes.explanation: Built-in reports and Analytics then let you monitor that traceability in real time.
notes.example: Like a parcel’s tracking number followed from order to doorstep, but for a requirement moving through code, build and release.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About end-to-end traceability” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure DevOps supports end-to-end traceability by linking various objects in your development process, such as work items, branches, commits, pull requests, builds, and releases. You can use built-in reports and Analytics to monitor traceability in real time.

notes.front: What does the requirements traceability matrix ensure?
notes.back: That all requirements defined for a system are tested in the test protocols.
notes.explanation: Requirements traceability rests on associating requirements with test cases, bugs and code changes.
notes.example: Like a table ticking each requirement off against the tests that cover it, kept inside Azure DevOps.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About end-to-end traceability”, “Requirements Traceability Matrix” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A fundamental aspect of requirements traceability is the association of requirements to test cases, bugs, and code changes. The Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) ensures that all requirements defined for a system are tested in the test protocols.

notes.front: What is bug traceability in Azure DevOps test results?
notes.back: Seeing a bug and its test result together in the Tests tab, with linked requirements shown in the Work Items tab.
notes.explanation: The bug, the test result and the requirements they touch sit in the same context.
notes.example: Like a bug report that arrives with its failing test run and the user story it breaks, all on one screen.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About end-to-end traceability”, “Bug traceability” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can see the bug and the test result together in the Tests tab, in the same context. The Work Items tab also shows any requirements that are linked to the test result.

notes.front: What is source traceability in Azure DevOps?
notes.back: Viewing the code changes committed in a build or release, through the timeline or pipeline view, to find a test failure’s likely root cause.
notes.explanation: It works back from the pipeline run to the commits it contained.
notes.example: Like reading `git log` between two releases, but opened from the pipeline run whose tests failed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About end-to-end traceability”, “Source traceability” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Based on the build or release pipeline, you can choose the timeline or pipeline view to see the committed code changes. You can analyze the code changes to identify the potential root cause of the test failure.

notes.front: What is quality traceability through test analytics?
notes.back: Using Test Analytics for builds and releases to track the quality of requirements and test failures.
notes.explanation: The traceability overview points to Test Analytics for exactly these three things: builds and releases, requirement quality and test failures.
notes.example: Like a school report per subject, but one per requirement, built from pipeline test results.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About end-to-end traceability”, “Test Analytics” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For more information about Test Analytics for builds and releases, tracking the quality of requirements, and test failures, see Test Analytics.

notes.front: What are default email subscriptions in Azure DevOps?
notes.back: Email subscriptions that are predefined and switched on automatically, covering the most common notification scenarios.
notes.explanation: They are the out-of-box notifications, in place before anyone creates a subscription of their own.
notes.example: Like the payment alerts a bank sends every customer unless they turn them off, but for Azure DevOps events.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About notifications”, “Default email subscriptions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Many useful email subscriptions are predefined and automatically enabled in the system. These resources and are referred to as **default subscriptions**. Default subscriptions provide out-of-box (OOB) support for the most common notification scenarios.

notes.front: What is a custom service hook subscription in Azure DevOps notifications?
notes.back: A subscription that notifies a third-party service whenever an Azure DevOps event matches it.
notes.explanation: It is the notification route for integrating third-party services, rather than sending email.
notes.example: Like an email subscription, but the recipient is an outside ticketing system instead of a person’s inbox.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About notifications”, “Custom service hook subscriptions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use service hooks subscriptions to integrate with third-party services. When an Azure DevOps event matches a service hook subscription, the third-party service receives a notification.

notes.front: GitHub flow is a {{c1::lightweight, branch-based}} workflow.
notes.explanation: GitHub describes it as useful for everyone, not just developers.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub flow”, “Introduction”
notes.evidence: flow is a lightweight, branch-based workflow. The {% data variables.product.prodname_dotcom %} flow is useful for everyone, not just developers.

notes.front: In GitHub flow, why should each commit ideally contain one isolated, complete change?
notes.back: It makes the change easy to revert if you decide to take a different approach.
notes.explanation: Reverting a commit then undoes that one change and nothing else.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub flow”, “Make changes”
notes.evidence: Ideally, each commit contains an isolated, complete change. This makes it easy to revert your changes if you decide to take a different approach.

notes.front: When you merge a pull request in GitHub flow, what does GitHub retain?
notes.back: The history of comments and commits in the pull request.
notes.explanation: That history helps future contributors understand your changes.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub flow”, “Merge your pull request”
notes.evidence: retains the history of comments and commits in the pull request to help future contributors understand your changes.

notes.front: In GitHub flow, why delete your branch after merging the pull request?
notes.back: It shows the work on the branch is complete and stops anyone accidentally using old branches.
notes.explanation: Nothing is lost: the pull request and its commit history are not deleted.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub flow”, “Delete your branch”
notes.evidence: This indicates that the work on the branch is complete and prevents you or others from accidentally using old branches. For more information, see AUTOTITLE. Don't worry about losing information. Your pull request and commit history will not be deleted.

notes.front: What does a keyword such as `fixes:` with an issue do in a GitHub pull request?
notes.back: It automatically closes the associated issue.
notes.explanation: A plain mention of the issue only creates a reference between the two.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About issues”, “About integration with GitHub”
notes.evidence: Mentioning an issue in another issue or pull request will create references between them and using keywords, like `fixes:`, in your pull requests will automatically close the associated issues.

notes.front: How do GitHub Projects use your issues to track work?
notes.back: All your issue metadata is available in your projects, so you can build views and filters of your work.
notes.explanation: Projects is strongly integrated with issues for planning and tracking a team’s work.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About issues”, “Using Projects to plan and track your work”
notes.evidence: is strongly integrated with issues to plan and track the work for your team. All your issue metadata is available in your projects, allowing you to create views and filters to represent your work.

notes.front: How do you reference a GitHub pull request from an Azure Boards work item’s text?
notes.back: Type `!` in a rich-text field or comment, then pick the pull request from a connected repository.
notes.explanation: The picker inserts the chosen pull request as a clickable link.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Link GitHub commits, pull requests, branches, and issues to work items in Azure Boards”, “Mention GitHub pull requests by using !” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use `!` mentions to reference and discuss GitHub pull requests directly from any work item rich-text field or discussion comment. When you type `!` in a text field, a picker appears that you can use to search for and select a GitHub pull request from a connected repository.

notes.front: When Azure Pipelines `YAML` builds a GitHub repository, which links can it create automatically on associated work items?
notes.back: Integrated in build links.
notes.explanation: This gives GitHub repositories the same build traceability that Azure Repos already has.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Link GitHub commits, pull requests, branches, and issues to work items in Azure Boards”, “View build status for YAML pipelines (Integrated in build)” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When you use Azure Pipelines YAML to build code hosted in a GitHub repository, you can automatically create Integrated in build links on associated work items. This feature provides build traceability for GitHub repos, achieving parity with the experience available for Azure Repos.

notes.front: To how many Azure DevOps organisations and projects can you connect one GitHub repository?
notes.back: Only one organisation and project.
notes.explanation: Connecting the same repository to projects in two or more organisations can cause unexpected `AB#` mention linking.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is the Azure Boards-GitHub integration?”, “Restrictions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can connect a GitHub repository to only one Azure DevOps organization and project. If you connect the same GitHub repository to projects defined in two or more Azure DevOps organizations, you might experience unexpected AB# mention linking.

notes.front: Why does connecting one GitHub repository to two Azure DevOps organisations confuse `AB#` links?
notes.back: Work item IDs aren’t unique across organisations, so both may try to link the same ID.
notes.explanation: `AB#12`, for example, could match a work item in either organisation.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Connect Azure Boards to GitHub (cloud)”, “Connect to multiple Azure DevOps organizations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Work item IDs aren't unique across organizations, so AB#12 could match a work item in either organization. Both organizations might attempt to link to the matching ID, causing confusion.

notes.front: You connect Azure Boards to GitHub with a personal access token. What must you configure so it can list repositories from an organisation that uses `SAML` authentication?
notes.back: Single sign-on for the token on your GitHub account.
notes.explanation: Single sign-on is required to list repositories from such an organisation.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Connect Azure Boards to GitHub (cloud)”, “Authentication options” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you connect with a PAT, configure single sign-on (SSO) for it on your GitHub account. SSO is required to list repositories from an organization that uses SAML authentication.

notes.front: By default, which state does `Fixes AB#123` move work item 123 to?
notes.back: The first state in the Resolved category or, if there is none, the first state in the Completed category.
notes.explanation: The keywords `fix`, `fixes` and `fixed` all behave this way.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Link GitHub commits, pull requests, branches, and issues to work items in Azure Boards”, “Use AB# to link from GitHub to Azure Boards work items” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By default, work items referenced with ``fix``, ``fixes``, or ``fixed`` transition to the first state associated with the Resolved category. If no such state exists in the current process, the system instead transitions the work item to the first state in the Completed category.

notes.front: What does `Closed AB#1234` in a pull request description do to work item 1234?
notes.back: Links it and moves it to the Closed state.
notes.explanation: A state name that isn’t recognised is matched to a workflow category such as Resolved or Completed instead.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Link GitHub commits, pull requests, branches, and issues to work items in Azure Boards”, “Use AB# to link from GitHub to Azure Boards work items” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When a pull request description includes a valid state name, for example, ``Closed AB#1234``, the system updates the referenced work item to that specific state. If the state name isn't recognized directly, Azure Boards tries to match it to a workflow category like ``Resolved`` or ``Completed``.

notes.front: A GitHub pull request is linked to a work item. What links to the work item automatically when the pull request is merged?
notes.back: The resulting merge commit.
notes.explanation: It is one of the GitHub events that update a work item’s links automatically, with no manual step.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Link GitHub commits, pull requests, branches, and issues to work items in Azure Boards”, “Automatic link updates” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Merge commit | After the pull request is merged, the resulting merge commit automatically links to the work item.

notes.front: When you create a GitHub branch from a work item with New GitHub branch, what does Azure Boards do?
notes.back: Creates the branch in the chosen GitHub repository and links it to the work item.
notes.explanation: The branch is tied to its work item from the moment it exists.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Link GitHub commits, pull requests, branches, and issues to work items in Azure Boards”, “Create GitHub branch from work item” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Boards creates the branch in the specified GitHub repository and links it to the work item.

notes.front: Which three statuses do GitHub pull request insights show beside a linked pull request?
notes.back: Draft status, review status and checks status.
notes.explanation: Checks status, for example, shows whether checks are passing, failing or pending.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Link GitHub commits, pull requests, branches, and issues to work items in Azure Boards”, “GitHub pull request insights” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Draft status**: Shows whether the pull request is still a draft. - **Review status**: Shows whether the pull request needs review, is approved, or has changes requested. - **Checks status**: Shows whether CI checks are passing, failing, or pending.
uses: GitHub pull request insights on a work item

notes.front: What must you accept before GitHub pull request insights appear on work items?
notes.back: The Azure Boards app’s updated permissions for read and write access to Checks.
notes.explanation: You accept them on the Azure Boards app in GitHub.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Link GitHub commits, pull requests, branches, and issues to work items in Azure Boards”, “Prerequisites for pull request insights” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To see pull request insights, go to the Azure Boards app in GitHub and accept the updated permissions for read and write access to Checks.
uses: GitHub pull request insights on a work item

notes.front: Which three build link types can you add from a work item?
notes.back: Build, Found in build and Integrated in build.
notes.explanation: You pick one of them in the Add link dialog and then specify the build number.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Link work items to objects”, “Link work items to builds” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: From the Add link dialog, choose one of the build link types: **Build**, **Found in build**, **Integrated in build**. Specify the build number.

notes.front: Which kind of release pipeline does a work item’s Deployment control need?
notes.back: A Classic release pipeline; release stages defined in `YAML` are not supported.
notes.explanation: Release stages defined in a `YAML` pipeline can’t be linked to it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Link work items to objects”, “Deployment control” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Deployment control requires configuration of a Classic release pipeline. It doesn't support linking to release stages defined for a YAML pipeline.

notes.front: What is it called when automated tests, linked to test cases, are used to track the quality of requirements?
notes.back: Planned testing.
notes.explanation: Linking the automated tests to test cases also lets you run them from Test Plans.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About end-to-end traceability”, “Manual and automated testing” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can also link them to test cases in a test plan and run them from Test Plans. By using this approach, you can track the quality of your requirements with automated tests, which is called *planned testing*.

notes.front: What do requirements traceability reports help a team measure?
notes.back: The quality and completeness of its requirements, and its readiness for delivery.
notes.explanation: They show how the phases of the development process are related and documented.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About end-to-end traceability”, “Requirements traceability reports” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Requirements traceability reports show how different phases of a development process are related and documented. They help teams measure the quality and completeness of their requirements and assess their readiness for delivery.

notes.front: How are Azure DevOps notifications delivered?
notes.back: By email or by service hook, according to the delivery properties in the subscription.
notes.explanation: A notification is generated for every match between an event and a subscription’s filter conditions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About notifications” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A notification is generated for every subscription/event match that meets the filter conditions. Notifications are delivered through email or service hook, based on the delivery properties defined in the subscription.

notes.front: Azure DevOps global notifications apply to {{c1::all projects}} defined for an organisation or collection.
notes.explanation: Global here means organisation-wide: every project, not one team or one project.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About notifications”, “Global notifications” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Global notifications apply to all projects defined for an organization or collection.

notes.front: Can one user opt out of a default email subscription without affecting teammates?
notes.back: Yes; the other team members remain subscribed.
notes.explanation: Administrators choose which default subscriptions to offer, and individuals can then opt out of any of them.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About notifications”, “Default email subscriptions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: An organization or team administrator can choose which of the default subscriptions to make available to their users. For more information, see Manage notifications for a team, project, or organization. Individual users can choose to opt out of any default subscription while other team members remain subscribed.

notes.front: A developer puts `AB#57` only in a pull request’s title, and no link appears on work item 57. What should they do?
notes.back: A) Put `AB#57` in the pull request description.
notes.choices:
A) Put `AB#57` in the pull request description
B) Put `AB#57` in a pull request comment
C) Keep the title and add `#57` to it
D) Rename the branch to `AB#57`
notes.choicesExplained: B: a mention in a comment doesn’t create a link either. C: `#57` is GitHub’s own issue reference, not an Azure Boards link. D: the documented places are commit messages, pull request descriptions and issue descriptions, not branch names.
notes.explanation: `AB#` in a title or comment creates no link; the description is one of the places that does.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Link GitHub commits, pull requests, branches, and issues to work items in Azure Boards”, “Use AB# to link from GitHub to Azure Boards work items” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Add `AB#{ID}` to a commit message, pull request description, or issue description. 1. Push the commit or save the pull request or issue. 1. Open the work item to confirm the link appears in the Development section. Using `AB#ID` in a comment or in a pull request title doesn't create a link on the work item.

notes.front: A commit message reads `Adds search, AB#77`. What happens to work item 77 once the commit is pushed?
notes.back: D) It is linked, and its state does not change.
notes.choices:
A) It moves to the first Resolved state
B) It moves to Closed
C) Nothing: a mention needs a keyword to link
D) It is linked, and its state does not change
notes.choicesExplained: A: that needs a keyword such as `fixes` before the mention. B: that needs the state name `Closed` before the mention. C: a bare `AB#` mention is enough to create the link.
notes.explanation: Without a state name or a keyword such as `fixes`, an `AB#` mention only links.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Link GitHub commits, pull requests, branches, and issues to work items in Azure Boards”, “Use AB# to link from GitHub to Azure Boards work items” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Adds a new feature, AB#123. | Links Azure Boards work item 123. No state transition occurs.

notes.front: A pull request with `Fixes AB#20` in its description is merged into a release branch, not the default branch. What happens to work item 20?
notes.back: B) It is linked, but its state does not change.
notes.choices:
A) It is linked and moves to the first Resolved state
B) It is linked, but its state does not change
C) It is neither linked nor moved
D) It is linked and moves to Closed
notes.choicesExplained: A: transitions apply only when the pull request is merged into the default branch. C: linking still works when you target other branches. D: `Closed` would need the state name, and no transition happens here anyway.
notes.explanation: Links still work for other target branches, but the transition rules wait for a merge into the default branch.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Link GitHub commits, pull requests, branches, and issues to work items in Azure Boards”, “Use AB# to link from GitHub to Azure Boards work items” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can still link work items and target other branches, but state transition rules don't apply unless the pull request is merged into the default branch.

notes.front: Last night’s build has a failing test, and you want to see which committed code changes might have caused it. Which kind of traceability is that?
notes.back: C) Source traceability.
notes.choices:
A) Bug traceability
B) The requirements traceability matrix
C) Source traceability
D) Planned testing
notes.choicesExplained: A: bug traceability shows the bug with its test result and linked requirements. B: the matrix checks that every requirement is tested. D: planned testing tracks requirement quality with automated tests linked to test cases.
notes.explanation: Source traceability goes from the build or release to its committed changes to find a test failure’s likely root cause.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About end-to-end traceability”, “Source traceability” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: you can choose the timeline or pipeline view to see the committed code changes. You can analyze the code changes to identify the potential root cause of the test failure.

notes.front: A tester wants the bug they filed, the failed test result and the requirement behind it in one place. Which kind of traceability is that?
notes.back: D) Bug traceability.
notes.choices:
A) Source traceability
B) Automatic link updates
C) The requirements traceability matrix
D) Bug traceability
notes.choicesExplained: A: source traceability shows the committed code changes behind a build. C: the matrix checks that all requirements are tested. B: automatic link updates add or remove code links on a work item after GitHub events.
notes.explanation: Bug traceability shows the bug and the test result together, and the Work Items tab adds the linked requirements.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About end-to-end traceability”, “Bug traceability” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can see the bug and the test result together in the Tests tab, in the same context. The Work Items tab also shows any requirements that are linked to the test result.

notes.front: An auditor asks you to show that every requirement defined for the system is tested. What should you use?
notes.back: A) The requirements traceability matrix.
notes.choices:
A) The requirements traceability matrix
B) A default email subscription
C) GitHub pull request insights
D) Source traceability
notes.choicesExplained: D: source traceability looks for the code change behind a test failure. B: a default subscription sends notifications. C: pull request insights show a linked pull request’s status.
notes.explanation: Ensuring all requirements are tested in the test protocols is exactly what the matrix does.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About end-to-end traceability”, “Requirements Traceability Matrix” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) ensures that all requirements defined for a system are tested in the test protocols.
uses: GitHub pull request insights on a work item

notes.front: Whenever a build completes, your team wants a message in an outside chat service. What do you set up in Azure DevOps?
notes.back: D) A custom service hook subscription.
notes.choices:
A) A custom email subscription
B) A default email subscription
C) A personal notification for each member
D) A custom service hook subscription
notes.choicesExplained: B: default subscriptions are predefined email notifications. C: personal notifications are managed by and for one user, not sent to an outside service. A: a custom email subscription emails organisation or team members, not an outside service.
notes.explanation: A service hook subscription sends the notification to a third-party service when a matching event occurs.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About notifications”, “Custom service hook subscriptions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use service hooks subscriptions to integrate with third-party services. When an Azure DevOps event matches a service hook subscription, the third-party service receives a notification.

notes.front: You need to change a notification that applies to every project in your Azure DevOps organisation. Which role do you need?
notes.back: D) Member of the Project Collection Administrators group.
notes.choices:
A) Team Administrator
B) Member of the Project Administrators group
C) The User role
D) Member of the Project Collection Administrators group
notes.choicesExplained: A: a Team Administrator can manage team notifications only. B: project administrators can manage team and project notifications, not global ones. C: the User role manages personal notifications.
notes.explanation: The notification types table lists only Project Collection Administrators against global notifications.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About notifications”, “Notification types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Personal notifications | User | | Team notifications | Team Administrator, or member of the Project Administrators group or Project Collection Administrators group | | Project notifications | Member of the Project Administrators group or Project Collection Administrators group | | Global notifications | Member of the Project Collection Administrators group

notes.front: Halfway through a change on your branch, you want colleagues’ advice before you finish. What does GitHub flow suggest?
notes.back: D) Open a pull request and mark it as a draft.
notes.choices:
A) Merge the branch, then ask for review
B) Push the change straight to the default branch
C) Wait until the change is complete before opening a pull request
D) Open a pull request and mark it as a draft
notes.choicesExplained: A: in GitHub flow you merge only once the pull request is approved. B: the branch exists so work doesn’t affect the default branch. C: a draft pull request is exactly for feedback before completion.
notes.explanation: GitHub flow is branch-based, and a draft pull request asks for feedback on the branch before the work is done.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub flow”, “Create a pull request”
notes.evidence: If you want early feedback or advice before you complete your changes, you can mark your pull request as a draft.

notes.front: When adding repositories to an Azure Boards connection, the list of GitHub repositories comes up empty. Your organisation restricts third-party applications. What should an owner do?
notes.back: D) Approve the Azure Boards app in the organisation’s OAuth app policy.
notes.choices:
A) Add `AB#` mentions to the repository’s commits
B) Connect the repository to a second Azure DevOps organisation
C) Accept the Checks permissions for pull request insights
D) Approve the Azure Boards app in the organisation’s OAuth app policy
notes.choicesExplained: B: a repository should be connected to only one organisation. C: Checks permissions enable pull request insights, not repository listing. A: mentions link work items once a connection exists.
notes.explanation: Restricted third-party access can leave the list empty or cause an error, so the app must be allowed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Install the Azure Boards app for GitHub”, “Check your third-party application access policy” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If third-party access is restricted, adding repositories from Azure DevOps can show an empty list or produce an error. To enable access: 1. In GitHub, open your organization and go to **Settings** > **OAuth app policy**. 1. Approve the Azure Boards app specifically (recommended), or remove restrictions for all third-party applications.

notes.front: You are connecting Azure Boards to repositories on GitHub Enterprise Server. Which authentication option is the preferred one?
notes.back: C) OAuth, which requires registration.
notes.choices:
A) A personal access token
B) GitHub credentials
C) OAuth, which requires registration
D) A GitHub.com user account
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: both are supported for GitHub Enterprise Server, but not marked as preferred. D: the GitHub.com user account is the recommended option for GitHub.com, not for Enterprise Server.
notes.explanation: For GitHub Enterprise Server the options are OAuth, a personal access token or GitHub credentials, and OAuth is marked preferred.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Connect Azure Boards to GitHub (cloud)”, “Authentication options” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: GitHub.com user account (Recommended) - Personal access token (PAT) :::column-end::: :::column span="":::   - OAuth (preferred, registration required) - PAT - GitHub credentials

notes.front: A product owner wants to see, from the work item, whether its linked GitHub pull request has changes requested, without opening GitHub. What provides that?
notes.back: A) GitHub pull request insights in the Development section.
notes.choices:
A) GitHub pull request insights in the Development section
B) An issue dependency on the pull request
C) A default email subscription
D) The Deployment control
notes.choicesExplained: B: issue dependencies record blocking between GitHub issues. C: default subscriptions send email notifications, not status on the work item. D: the Deployment control shows release stages.
notes.explanation: Pull request insights show draft, review and checks status beside the linked pull request.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is the Azure Boards-GitHub integration?”, “Integration features” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: View draft status, review status, and Checks status for linked GitHub pull requests directly from the Development section.
uses: GitHub pull request insights on a work item
Development section of a work item

notes.front: You link a work item to a page in the project wiki. Which link type category is that?
notes.back: A) Wiki.
notes.choices:
A) Wiki
B) Requirement
C) Remote work
D) Code
notes.choicesExplained: D: Code links point to branches, changesets, commits, pull requests, tags or versioned items. B: Requirement links point to a storyboard through a web address. C: Remote work links point to work items in a different organisation.
notes.explanation: Each link type category names the kind of object at the other end; a wiki page has its own.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Link work items to objects”, “Types of links” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Requirement | Connects a work item to a storyboard through URL. | | Test | Connects a work item to a test attachment or result. | | Wiki | Connects a work item to a wiki page.

notes.front: A developer wants each new branch linked to its user story without typing any mention. What should they do?
notes.back: C) Create the branch from the work item.
notes.choices:
A) Add the story as an issue dependency
B) Mention the story in a pull request comment
C) Create the branch from the work item
D) Put the story’s ID in the pull request title
notes.choicesExplained: B: mentions in comments don’t create links. A: issue dependencies relate GitHub issues to each other. D: an `AB#` mention in a title creates no link either.
notes.explanation: A branch created from a work item is linked to it automatically with the Branch link type.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About end-to-end traceability”, “Create a branch and pull request from a work item” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can create a branch from a work item by opening the work item card menu on the product board or by selecting Create a branch in the work item form. The branch is automatically linked to the work item with the Branch link type.

notes.front: Your company wants its GitHub.com repositories linked to Azure Boards through a connection that doesn’t run as any one employee. What should you use?
notes.back: C) The Azure Boards app for GitHub.
notes.choices:
A) A personal access token belonging to an administrator
B) A connection with one engineer’s GitHub.com user account
C) The Azure Boards app for GitHub
D) An OAuth registration for GitHub Enterprise Server
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: both act with one person’s identity. D: OAuth registration is the preferred option for GitHub Enterprise Server, not GitHub.com.
notes.explanation: The app authenticates and operates as the app rather than as an individual.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is the Azure Boards-GitHub integration?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The app provides a more streamlined configuration experience and has the advantage of authenticating and operating as the app rather than an individual.

notes.front: A team keeps its code in a Git repository on a hosting service other than GitHub or Azure Repos. Can it use `AB#` linking with Azure Boards?
notes.back: B) No: only GitHub and Azure Repos Git repositories are supported.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, after installing the Azure Boards app for GitHub
B) No: only GitHub and Azure Repos Git repositories are supported
C) Yes, through a personal access token connection
D) Yes, if the repository is connected to only one organisation
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D: none of these changes the restriction; Azure DevOps doesn’t integrate with other Git repositories at all.
notes.explanation: The integration is limited to GitHub repositories and Azure Repos Git repositories.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is the Azure Boards-GitHub integration?”, “Restrictions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure DevOps can only integrate with GitHub repositories or Azure Repos Git repositories. Integration with other Git repositories isn't supported.

notes.front: A GitHub issue has turned into an open-ended conversation better suited to a discussion. What can you do with it?
notes.back: Convert the issue to a discussion.
notes.explanation: Some conversations suit GitHub Discussions better than issues, and conversion moves them there.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About issues”, “Comparing issues and discussions”
notes.evidence: When a conversation in an issue is better suited for a discussion, you can convert the issue to a discussion.

notes.front: How do `Fixes AB#123, AB#124` and `Fixes AB#123, Fixes AB#124` differ?
notes.back: Both link both items; the first transitions only 123, the second transitions both.
notes.explanation: The keyword applies to the `AB#` reference that follows it, so each item needs its own.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Link GitHub commits, pull requests, branches, and issues to work items in Azure Boards”, “Use AB# to link from GitHub to Azure Boards work items” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Transitions only the first item, 123, to the Resolved workflow state category or, if none is defined, then the Completed workflow state category. | | Fixes AB#123, Fixes AB#124, Fixes AB#125 | Links to Azure Boards work items 123, 124, and 125. Transitions all items

notes.front: On a work item form, how does the Development section differ from the Deployment section?
notes.back: Development opens linked branches, commits, pull requests or builds; Deployment shows release information for work items in a build being released.
notes.explanation: Together they carry a requirement from code through to release stages.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About end-to-end traceability”, “Deploy changes into production” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Deployment section: Find release information for work items associated with a Git commit that's part of a build being released.
uses: Development section of a work item
